title: Orchestrating Regeneration: How Temporality and Spatiality Shape Regenerative Strategies for Biodiversity
journal: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Companies are increasingly called to move beyond mitigating their environmental impacts and adopt regenerative approaches that enhance the health of socio‐ecological systems. However, little is known about how such ambitions are translated into corporate strategy. A growing literature underscores the role of spatiotemporal scales in business strategies, particularly within the context of sustainability. This study investigates how companies interpret and combine spatial and temporal dimensions in developing regenerative strategies for biodiversity (RSB). The study adopts a qualitative research design by examining seven multinational companies embracing a regenerative business model in biodiversity‐salient sectors. Data were gathered through semi‐structured interviews with key managers, complemented with corporate and archival documents, and analysed abductively using the Gioia methodology. The analysis reveals three distinct yet coexisting organizing logics through which companies develop RSB: Dependency Management, Stewardship & Advocacy, and Trust‐Building. Each logic rests on a distinct coupling of temporal and spatial orientations, in which objective and processual interpretations of time, and objective and relational interpretations of space, intertwine in different ways. Companies combine these logics, highlighting that the formation of regenerative strategies is an adaptive configuration of interrelated practices enacted across heterogeneous temporal and spatial scales. The study contributes to research on RSB by advancing that strategy formation is a plural and dynamic process, and that regenerative strategizing entails the coexistence and interplay of multiple logics, each underpinned by different spatiotemporal orientations.

title: Towards post-growth policymaking: Barriers and enablers for wellbeing economy and Doughnut economics initiatives
abstract: Providing wellbeing for all while safeguarding planetary boundaries may require governments to pursue post-growth policies. An important question is the extent to which government-led post-growth initiatives can be transformative within the existing institutional context. Initial empirical studies have highlighted some of the limitations these initiatives currently face, but a broader empirical assessment of the underlying barriers and enablers across institutional contexts is still lacking. To address this gap, we examine wellbeing economy and Doughnut economics government initiatives across governance scales in Europe, New Zealand, and Canada. To identify barriers and enablers as well as priorities for future action, we develop and apply a framework that captures systemic and political dimensions to analyze the data. Overall, our results suggest that the overarching economic growth paradigm severely limits the initiatives’ scope of action. Important enablers of existing initiatives in our study include crises, the political agency of key individuals, and high-level political support. Civil servants who promote growth-critical perspectives often face tensions: they need to appeal to broad stakeholder groups while avoiding co-optation. To create the political and organizational conditions for transformative policy change we suggest focusing on two areas: fostering a critical consciousness of growth hegemony in society, and institutionally embedding post-growth-aligned political priorities whenever there are political windows of opportunity. Strengthening government-led post-growth initiatives will also require stronger engagement with — and pressure from — civil society.

title: Exploring the potential and limits of non-profit-maximising business models in transformative change: Insights from Italian fashion small and medium enterprises
Regenerative Business Between Normative Ambition and Managerial Practice: A Systematic Review Through the Integrated Management Model
abstract: ABSTRACT As the regenerative rhetoric spreads across research and practice, management literature remains fragmented, with no coherent account of how regenerative principles are defined, governed, and enacted at the organizational level. This systematic literature review synthesizes 36 peer‐reviewed articles (2017–2025) through the lens of the Integrated Management Model, structuring regenerative business along normative, strategic, and operational levels. The analysis shows that the field's coherence is unevenly distributed: it converges on a shared normative core of ecological worldview, systemic purpose, and net positive contribution to socio‐ecological systems, while the strategic mechanisms and measurement systems that would translate that core into practice remain comparatively undeveloped. Regenerative business thus emerges less as an accomplished paradigm shift than as a discourse defined by the shift it pursues. We identify central tensions and propose a research agenda to close the distance between its normative ambition and its managerial means.

title: Enjoying more years of good life while reducing resource use and emissions? A global panel analysis 1990–2019
authors: Duro, Juan Antonio; Galiana, Pau; Soldevila, M. Victòria; Piñol, Josep M.; Martín, Mónica; Sardà, Jordi; Ponce-Alifonso, Xavier; Farré Albendea, Fco Javier
abstract: Sustainability is essentially about enabling everyone to live a good life within planetary boundaries. Analysing this goal is hindered by problems of definition, measurement, and the large number of relevant factors. Comprehensive assessments of countries' resource requirements and emissions (i.e. their socioeconomic metabolism or SEM) related to human wellbeing are missing. To advance the field, we develop a multi-dimensional set of SEM indicators and analyse its relationship with the number of ‘years of good life’ (YoGL) of their inhabitants. The wellbeing indicator ‘YoGL’ measures years a person can expect to live above absolute poverty while enjoying health and life satisfaction. A descriptive analysis of ~110 countries from 1990 to 2019 reveals saturation curves: strong association of SEM and YoGL at low and weaker relations at higher levels of SEM and wellbeing. In a range of panel analyses we introduce mediating factors capturing how countries' provisioning systems turn resources into well-being relevant services (e.g. GDP, education, pollution or inequality). The association between SEM indicators and YoGL mostly disappears or even becomes inverse when mediating factors are considered. GDP is positively associated with YoGL in many but not all analyses. Education is positively and air pollution negatively associated with YoGL when the other explanatory variables are controlled. A cluster analysis of high-YoGL countries identifies a group enjoying highest YoGL at intermediate levels of resource use and emissions. Our results imply that raising wellbeing for all while reducing resource use and emissions will require moving beyond simple ‘decoupling’ and resource-use efficiency approaches.

title: Ecological macroeconomics models? Caveat emptor
abstract: Ecological Macroeconomic Integrated Assessment Models (EM-IAMs) have emerged as tools for exploring post-growth narratives and challenging the dominant discourse of continuous economic growth. Their use may be strategically advantageous: by employing modelling approaches that are epistemically legitimate within economics, EM-IAMs can contest the growth paradigm with their own tools. Yet, the framing of socio-ecological processes in EM-IAMs, through quantification and evaluative logics, risks interfering with the other goal of EM-IAMs; to address social inequality and injustices. As such, EM-IAMs risk operating as what ecologist Langdon Winner coined as ‘conceptual Trojan horse’. We question whether EM-IAMs may truly provide “robust modelling tools to explore alternative future scenarios, enabling the ex-ante evaluation of direct and indirect effects of policies on well-being, employment, and the ecosystem” (Ecological Economics, 2025). Our doubts rest upon complexity that does not reduce uncertainty, the politics of model simplification, the limitations of EM-IAM models for aspects that resist quantification, the reinforcement of historical power imbalances, and, ultimately, the performative effects of models themselves. We suggest that, rather than extending EM-IAMs to incorporate well-being analysis, we should adopt a different approach to modelling, learning from ecological values; appreciating diversity, variability in space and time, self-regulation, and entanglements.

title: Housing stock evolution and planetary boundaries: Forecasting the sector's socio-metabolic and emissions trajectory to enable transition management toward absolute sustainability
abstract: Housing stock growth is essential for accommodating population growth while threatening planetary sustainability. Mitigation literature focuses on building-level innovations, while a broader perspective is needed to assess the stock's efficiency in delivering housing services within ecological limits. This research proposes an interdisciplinary framework encompassing socio-metabolic research, advanced forecasting, and absolute sustainability. Applied to New Zealand's residential sector, we utilize 35 years of building consent data across three building typologies to map the stock's evolution, forecast its trajectory, and benchmark embodied emissions against planetary boundaries. Retrospective analysis indicates post-COVID-19 stabilization, following unprecedented sector growth, steady densification since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and 2016 zoning reforms, and a potential decline in construction quality since 2020. Forecasts through 2029 suggest townhouses will surpass detached housing in consented dwellings, while the latter continue to dominate consented gross floor area. During this period, the sector is anticipated to consume 14 Mt of building materials and emit 8 Mt of embodied emissions, currently exceeding its carbon planetary boundary by a factor of 7.5, while projected to reach 8.6 by 2029. Finally, typologies are assessed as provisioning systems highlighting townhouses' marginal superiority in affordability and environmental efficiency. Nevertheless, even the best-performing typology was found to require 11.9 t CO 2 -eq per capita, significantly exceeding the 1.7 t CO 2 -eq absolute sustainability limit. The findings indicate that neither technological efficiency nor affluence sufficiency alone can guide the sector toward absolute sustainability, highlighting the urgent need for combined interventions or exploration of alternative housing systems beyond traditional urban paradigms.

title: A framework for developing an emissions reduction roadmap for new residential buildings in urban Uganda: A demonstrative case study of detached bungalows
abstract: Considering the remaining global emissions budget is essential when regulating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the building sector, especially for emerging economies where the building stock is still undergoing rapid expansion. This study demonstrates a framework for developing an emissions reduction roadmap for detached bungalows in urban Uganda. A planetary boundary-based top-down benchmark for Uganda's housing emissions is derived. A hybrid life cycle GHG emissions assessment is conducted for a bungalow over 50 years. Context-specific emissions targets and reduction pathways are derived, forming the roadmap. The framework explores how a 71.6% emissions reduction requirement could be achieved over a 20-year period to remain below the 2°C warming threshold at an 83% risk-avoidance level. The demonstrative findings suggest that significant emissions reductions could be achieved by lowering embodied GHG emissions through sufficiency-oriented building design and low emissions-intensive construction materials and methods. Regulating dwelling stock growth and designing for optimal occupancy densities are identified as potentially important for achieving meaningful reductions. The framework highlights the importance of improving and scaling up Uganda's traditional earthen and bio-based materials to support reductions in embodied emissions. It further demonstrates the value of expressing assessment results using both floor area-based and per capita-based functional units to better account for house size in sufficiency-oriented design. The demonstrative application also highlights the importance of developing context-specific material life cycle inventory data and integrating emissions reduction strategies into Uganda's building policies to support refinement and implementation of the proposed reduction roadmap.

title: Europe at the crossroads: trading strategic autonomy for resilience under degrowth
Decoupling Economic Growth From Material Use: A Bibliometric Review and Research Agenda for Business Management Scholarship
abstract: ABSTRACT The imperative to decouple economic growth from resource consumption sits at the heart of current sustainability research, yet the role of businesses in this process has barely been explored. This paper presents a bibliometric analysis of 251 documents from the Web of Science (1998–2025) examining decoupling, the circular economy and material flow analysis. Drawing on co‐citation networks, keyword co‐occurrence, thematic mapping, bibliographic coupling and thematic evolution analysis using the Bibliometrix package in R, we map the intellectual structure and research dynamics of this domain. Three intellectual clusters emerge—planetary boundaries and degrowth, empirical decoupling analysis and social metabolism—alongside two active research fronts, whose intellectual core does not include authors primarily affiliated with business management. This is the central finding of the paper. We are dealing with a domain that has grown at a compound annual rate of 12.66% over nearly three decades, yet has done so without the systematic engagement of business management scholarship. Emerging topics—such as recycling, digital platforms and circular business models—point toward a future convergence. This review offers a business‐oriented bibliometric synthesis of the field and proposes a five‐strand research agenda for management scholars.

title: Multi-dimensional environmental impact assessment of China's dietary shift within planetary boundaries
Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life.

title: Sustainable Business Model Innovation Research: Bibliometric Structures and the Emerging Frontier of Regenerative Business Models (2016–2025)
journal: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
abstract: ABSTRACT This study presents a bibliometric mapping of sustainable business model innovation (SBMI) research, analysing 961 Scopus‐indexed documents (2016–2025) retrieved via a title‐field Boolean query and a four‐stage screening protocol. Circular, regenerative, and resilient business models are treated as distinct, related perspectives rather than sequential stages. The corpus shows a three‐phase growth trajectory: emergence, acceleration, and consolidation, with an overall compound annual growth rate of 24.5%. Knowledge production concentrates in European institutions, led by Sweden, the UK, and Italy, anchored by Lund University. Co‐citation (four clusters) and keyword co‐occurrence (five clusters) analyses reveal a field anchored in Osterwalder and Pigneur's business model canvas. The regenerative perspective remains bibliometrically marginal, appearing as an author keyword in only 2 of 961 documents. The study clarifies the boundaries separating these perspectives and proposes a structured research agenda, positioning regeneration as an emerging, not accomplished, frontier for sustainable business model innovation scholarship.

title: Frugal Innovation as an Environmentally Oriented Business Strategy: The Roles of Servant Leadership and Organizational Learning Capability
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how firms develop frugal innovation as an environmentally oriented business strategy that combines competitiveness with lower resource intensity. Drawing on sustainable business strategy research and using degrowth as an interpretive lens rather than a causal theory, we conceptualize frugal innovation as an organizational outcome centered on core functionalities, substantial cost reduction, and shared sustainable engagement. We test the roles of servant leadership and organizational learning capability using survey data from 450 manufacturing firms in Santa Catarina, Brazil. The results show that both servant leadership and organizational learning capability are positively associated with frugal innovation, with organizational learning capability exerting the stronger direct effect. Organizational learning capability also mediates the servant leadership–frugal innovation relationship, indicating that leadership also contributes to frugal innovation when relational conditions are translated into learning routines such as experimentation, dialogue, and participative decision‐making. Multi‐group analysis indicates that the structural relationships predicting frugal innovation are broadly stable across technological intensity levels, although the servant leadership–organizational learning capability link is stronger in medium to medium‐high technology firms. The study advances research on business strategy and the environment by empirically specifying organizational learning capability as a mediating mechanism linking servant leadership to frugal innovation. It also examines the stability of these relationships across technological intensity groups in an emerging‐economy manufacturing context.

title: An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
abstract: This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

title: How much is enough? Operationalizing perceived clothing sufficiency through wardrobe studies
Circular Economy and Supply Chain Performance Under Geopolitical Tensions: The Roles of Recycling Efficiency and Logistics Infrastructure Capability
abstract: ABSTRACT This study analyzed the effects of circular economy practices, resource self‐sufficiency capability, and organizational resilience capability on supply chain distribution performance in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region amid geopolitical tensions. The escalating geopolitical uncertainty, trade restrictions, and disrupted supply chains have illustrated the vulnerability of global supply chains, compelling organizations to implement measures that improve resource efficiency, resiliency, and sustainability over the long term. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was used in manufacturing and logistics firms, and data were collected from 320 manufacturing experts, supply chain managers, logistics experts, policy advisors, and sustainability officers across all six GCC countries. Smart PLS used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) to analyze the data, including measurement model evaluation to assess reliability and validity and structural model evaluation to assess the effects of direct, mediating, and moderating variables. With the aid of dynamic capability theory and closed‐loop supply chain theory, this study has come up with a synthesized model to describe the role of internal capabilities and circular practices in enhancing the outcomes of distribution. The study hypothesizes that recycling efficiency is a mediating factor that converts circular economy initiatives into actual operational advantages in terms of better material recovery, less reliance on external resources, and more predictable input flows. Moreover, logistics infrastructure capability is studied as a moderating factor reinforcing the relationship between recycling efficiency and distribution performance by making it able to revive efficient product returns, recovery, and reintegration processes. Based on empirical research data of companies that are working in GCC supply chains, the analysis aims to inform how companies can improve distribution efficiency and resilience and promote circular economy goals in a geopolitically uncertain context.

title: From mandatory disclosure data to organisational decision-making guided by planetary boundaries
abstract: Organisations currently lack operational methods to assess how their activities contribute to returning society to within Earth's safe operating space, considering that seven of the nine planetary boundaries are currently exceeded. Although the mandatory Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive of the European Union generates extensive compliance data, these disclosures remain disconnected from planetary boundary science. In this context, the study addresses two key knowledge gaps: (i) the methodological disconnect between mandatory sustainability reporting requirements and science-based environmental impact assessment frameworks, and (ii) the absence of implementation pathways in real organisational contexts. To bridge these gaps, an integrated framework was developed that exclusively uses mandatory European Sustainability Reporting Standards disclosure data as a starting point for an Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment following the Environmental Footprint Method. A case study focusing on the University of Coimbra demonstrates the framework. Results reveal significant environmental transgressions that are sensitive to the allocation principle applied. Under egalitarian allocation, impacts related to mineral depletion, land use, particulate matter, and climate change exceeded allocated capacity. Under the utilitarian allocation approach, the absolute magnitudes of exceedances decreased by about fourfold, while the ranking of the environmental problems remained the same. More than 88% of total environmental impacts originated from upstream value chain activities. This finding shifts sustainability priorities away from a narrow focus on operational efficiency towards procurement governance, particularly for infrastructure, equipment, food, and mobility. The study demonstrates that organisations already collecting compliance data possess the underlying data required for Absolute Environmental Sustainability Assessment, suggesting that an evolution in sustainability regulation, from transparency-based reporting towards absolute sustainability governance, is both technically achievable and operationally feasible.

title: Organizational Growth Reconsidered: A Systems‐Based Review and Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent years have witnessed a significant increase in post‐ and degrowth research, which explores the social and ecological consequences of, and alternatives to, economic growth. To date, however, the debate has primarily occurred at the macroeconomic level, leaving a gap in our understanding of the role of organizational growth in a post‐growth context. Therefore, in this paper, we review the general management and corporate sustainability literatures, which have long investigated organizational growth, to gain insights into the inputs, processes, and outputs of organizational growth across multiple levels of analysis. Drawing on these findings and adopting a systems perspective, we devise a research agenda for future growth‐critical research at the organizational level. We suggest that studying emergence, adaptation, interdependence, and feedback in relation to organizational growth has significant potential to advance the fields of both corporate sustainability and post‐ and degrowth. Additionally, our integrative review offers practical advice for managers and policymakers seeking to guide organizations toward post‐growth pathways.

title: Closing the Sustainable Development Implementation Gap at the Firm Level: A Diagnostic Instrument and Validation Protocol for SDG ‐Aligned, Planetary‐Boundary‐Bounded Firm Practice in Small and Medium‐Sized Enterprises
journal: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the United Nations 2030 Agenda's call for firm‐level Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) implementation, no validated diagnostic exists to assess whether small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) have developed the operating capability that SDG‐implementation adequacy requires against absolute biophysical reference points, rather than relative improvement against firm‐specific baselines. This paper develops Planetary Boundary Operating Capability (PBOC), a firm‐level diagnostic construct comprising three hierarchically structured sub‐capabilities, Scale‐aware Operations, Distribution‐just Practices, and Regenerative Allocation, grounded in the Daly–Farley ends–means hierarchy and the firm‐level planetary‐boundaries literature. PBOC measures institutionalised managerial capability oriented toward operating within absolute biophysical limits; it is a capability‐readiness proxy, not a certification that a firm operates within any planetary boundary, and is designed to be triangulated against objective environmental data. Its items directly operationalise targets under SDG 6 (water), SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 8 (decent work), SDG 12 (responsible consumption and production), SDG 13 (climate), SDG 15 (life on land), and SDG 17 (partnerships); SDGs 1 and 3 enter only as downstream outcomes used for nomological validation, under an explicit three‐tier scope taxonomy. We contribute (i) a theoretically derived candidate 36‐item instrument, including new items on boundary downscaling and firm‐level budget governance; (ii) a formal derivation of the scale–distribution–allocation sequence as a necessary‐condition structure, distinguished from additive and parallel alternatives; and (iii) a pre‐specified two‐phase validation protocol for Taiwanese SMEs, Phase 1 psychometric refinement (content validity, Q‐sort, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis) and Phase 2 nomological validation (partial least squares structural equation modelling and Necessary Condition Analysis), with target samples, competing‐model comparisons, common‐method‐bias remedies, and analytic thresholds fixed in advance. This is a study protocol: it reports the construct, instrument, hypotheses, and analysis plan; no data have yet been collected and no empirical results are reported. The protocol offers sustainable development scholarship a diagnostic for CSRD/ISSB/TNFD transition support and Necessary Condition Analysis as a method for adjudicating hierarchical SDG‐implementation claims.

title: The state of degrowth research and how to assess it
abstract: Abstract This article addresses two inter-related questions. First, are degrowth claims supported by empirical evidence? And second, how do we go about reviewing the literature to answer this question? We analyze five recent reviews on the state of degrowth research focusing on the more critical, outlier of the five studies, and compare it with the four others in terms of their findings and in terms of their approach to reviewing the literature. In terms of evidence, our main finding is that the core claim of degrowth research, that green growth is unlikely if not impossible, is well supported by now; tentative findings also support the feasibility of degrowth-oriented pathways. In terms of review practice, we find that a good review of an interdisciplinary sustainability field like degrowth should avoid disciplinary biases, be transparent about its own assumptions, and use methods that are fit for the purposes it sets for itself.

title: Regenerative business models in B Corps: seven multi-level criteria for identification, drivers of transition, and a maturity trajectory
abstract: The body of literature on regenerative business models is growing rapidly. Nevertheless, three significant gaps remain unresolved: no operational criteria distinguish regenerative enterprises from sustainable firms; the drivers enabling transition toward regeneration remain poorly understood; and only a few frameworks explain how regenerative practices develop within organizations. Together, these gaps hinder coherent understanding of regenerative enterprises. This research aims to address these gaps through an exploratory qualitative study based on multiple case studies of Italian B Corps. Following a multi-stage selection process, seven B Corps with regenerative characteristics were selected for in-depth analysis. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using an abductive approach and the Gioia methodology. The findings reveal that visionary leadership, organizational culture, and authentic purpose are the most significant drivers of regenerative transition, whereas regulatory and market pressures play a comparatively marginal role. This result diverges from the prevailing assumptions in the circular economy literature. The contribution of the paper is fourfold. First, it adapts the analytical logic of the Multi-Level Perspective (MLP) to the regeneration domain, providing an integrative framework that links individual, organizational, and institutional dimensions. Second, it develops and validates seven multi-level operational criteria distinguishing regenerative enterprises from advanced sustainability-oriented firms. Third, it identifies and organizes the main drivers of regenerative transition within a multilevel framework. Fourth, it introduces regenerative maturity as an emerging evolutionary path inferred from cross-case patterns among pioneering regenerative firms. Finally, the paper outlines several operational guidelines for managers and policymakers seeking to promote systemic regenerative transitions.

title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions
abstract: The dialectic relationship between the production of post-growth knowledge and ongoing construction of social reality is a complex one, but one that warrants attention. In this scoping review, we respond to the emergent interest in post-growth politics and theories of change. We aim to complement existing reviews of post-growth policy proposals and recommendations with an analysis of peer-reviewed studies on interventions – deliberate attempts by one state, market or civil society actor to influence another. Drawing on a socio-ecological systems leverage points perspective embedded within a political economy inspired mapping of social forces, we develop a conceptual framework for explaining strategic trade-offs made by actors to achieve various forms of depth. Our findings point to asymmetrical relationships between actors-executor pairs and a pattern of neoliberal subjectification in both intervention design and analytical focus. We also find that whilst post-growth interventions can readily achieve discursive depth, it is often accompanied by institutional shallowness and temporal fragility. We conclude with reflections on strategic implications for post-growth researchers and movements.

title: A Social and Solidarity Economy Network's Evolution on Sustainability Discourses: Weak Versus Strong Sustainability
abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores innovations concerning sustainability discourses in the case of a Social and Solidarity Economy (SSE) network. We analyse the incorporation of discursive elements characteristic of strong sustainability versus weak sustainability approaches in the different Solidarity Economy Principles Charters over time (2000, 2011, 2022), for the case of Spain's Red de Economía Alternativa y Solidaria (REAS; Alternative and Solidarity Economy Network). The methodology combines discourse analysis of the three charters following an abductive logic that moves iteratively between theory and data. Discursive fragments are coded along a four‐level sustainability continuum (from very weak to very strong), based on three criteria: capital substitutability, stance towards economic growth and conception of nature. The findings highlight that REAS's normative language and frames of reference have evolved towards the incorporation of an increasing number of discursive elements associated with a strong sustainability perspective, including concepts such as rights of nature or limits to growth. This study shows how REAS's sustainability discourse has evolved from a weak sustainability orientation towards normative elements characteristic of very strong sustainability; but translating this discursive shift into robust measurement indicators and substantial practical transformations remains a significant challenge.

title: Secure Enough? Sufficiency and Security in the New Geological and Geopolitical Reality
abstract: ABSTRACT This article advances sufficiency theorizing by examining its relationship with security in the contemporary geopolitical context. It engages three contextually situated discourses: sustainable development, ecological civilization, and degrowth, to explore how concerns over ecological limits intersect with emerging geopolitical and security challenges in the Anthropocene. To illustrate how global security dynamics materialize in specific places, the study draws on two examples of critical mineral extraction. Conceptually, the article distinguishes sufficiency , understood as a process of reducing global matter‐energy throughput to ecological limits, from geopolitical strategies of self‐sufficiency aimed at securing resource supply. Building on this distinction, it analyzes tensions between security‐driven growth and enoughness. The study argues that contemporary responses to geopolitical insecurity often reinforce extractive and expansionary logics, particularly through the securitization of critical raw materials, while global sufficiency foregrounds ecological limits as a condition for long‐term security. It concludes by suggesting that sufficiency may offer a provisional normative language through which the discourses of sustainable development, ecological civilization, and degrowth can address their shared concerns on the continuity of life, while acknowledging the political tensions and practical constraints involved in its realization.

title: UNCASExt – A systematic computational framework for uncertainty propagation and scope consistency in absolute environmental sustainability assessments (AESA)
abstract: Absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA) has gained increasing attention in environmental research and policymaking. However, its reliability is challenged by several sources of uncertainty that remain insufficiently accounted for, as well as by scope inconsistencies within the absolute sustainability ratio (ASR), which compares estimated environmental burdens with allocated carrying capacities for a given human activity. This work introduces UNCASExt , an extension of the UNCASE framework for systematically propagating uncertainty and ensuring scope consistency in AESA, together with a supporting open-source Python package, pyaesa . At country and sector levels, the computational framework formalizes allocation procedures that match the scope of allocated carrying capacities with that of estimated environmental burdens across three dimensions: impact pathway modeling; production-based versus consumption-based accounting; business-to-consumer (B2C) versus business-to-business (B2B) activities. It also incorporates temporal dynamics, supporting both retrospective and prospective assessments with either static steady-state or dynamic carrying capacities, including greenhouse gas budgets from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway transition scenarios. The framework is applied to a case study of electricity consumption in France over the period 2019–2060. The results show that mismatches between the functional units of estimated environmental burdens and allocated carrying capacities can lead to substantial underallocation, with a median factor of 4.6 × across all available sector-region pairs in the multi-regional input–output table EXIOBASE 3.10.2. Overall, UNCASExt and pyaesa provide a scalable solution to support AESA harmonization and a versatile way forward to bridge the gap between methodological guidelines and practical application.

title: Assessing absolute sustainability: An analysis of impact assessment tools
abstract: Impact investors require information on whether a company's impacts are consistent with global environmental and social limits, yet the impact assessment tools (IATs) available for this purpose remain methodologically heterogeneous and rarely reflect absolute sustainability. In this paper, we address this gap in two steps. First, we conduct a systematic literature review on absolute sustainability to derive criteria for how absolute sustainability should be reflected in IATs conceptually for investment decision-making. Second, we translate these criteria into an analytical framework comprising a descriptive and an evaluative layer, with the latter specifying 12 criteria across 5 dimensions with a four-level scale. We apply this framework to 15 IATs. We find that IATs differ substantially in methodological rigor and rarely integrate a full life cycle perspective, absolute global thresholds and their allocation, as well as temporal dynamics or evidence of causal contribution. We further identify interdependencies between IATs, indicating that they are complementary rather than substitutable. Because IATs pursue different objectives, the descriptive layer represents this variation, implying that the results should be interpreted as alignment with the concept of absolute sustainability rather than as a universal quality ranking. We conclude that IATs are not yet adequately equipped to support capital allocation aligned with absolute sustainability, and that closing this gap requires operationalizing thresholds, allocation, and causal attribution at the company level.

title: Theoretical Foundations for a Sustainability and Climate Change Strategic Leadership Typology: Towards Regenerative Leadership
abstract: Abstract The interlinked climate and ecological crises have profound implications for future human success. Temperatures are set to rise by 3–4 0 C by the end of the century and there is already a sixty-nine per cent global average biodiversity abundance loss since 1970. Most of our business and management literature continues to rely on traditional, anthropocentric, leadership and strategy theories as a route to change without considering the embedded, systemic, heterogeneous, and future-orientated nature of the problem. Given this multifaceted grand challenge, and the compounding lack of adequate business and management theoretical foundations for such research investigations, we propose six strategic leadership types (and their underpinning values and capabilities) that help to differentiate leadership for the complex climate and ecological crises we face. The leadership types, greenwash, resilience, eco-innovation, ecocentric visionary (sustainability), degrowth and regenerative leadership, are calibrated against known ontological and strategic perspectives, which provide plurality and fluidity of thought, allowing connection between the natural and social sciences, to aid understanding of research towards sustainability and climate change. We reframe the leadership literature by locating our theoretical contribution within environmental ethics, linking our understanding of the natural world, human ethics, and related business ethics, identifying regenerative leadership as the most ethical and most promising type.

title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate.

title: A Systematic Review of Degrowth Food‐Systems, Framework Conceptualisation and Thematic Tensions
abstract: ABSTRACT Degrowth food‐systems offer ways to address inequity, poor health, greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss arising from globally dominant industrial food‐systems. In this study, a systematic review of degrowth food‐system research literature was conducted in the Web of Science on 7 February 2025 to identify descriptions of degrowth food‐system attributes within research literature, develop a degrowth food‐system conceptual model based on identified thematic trends and identify priorities for future research based on an examination of thematic tensions emergent within the results. Records were eligible for review if they contained descriptions of degrowth food‐system attributes according to food‐system attributes present in a food‐system framework synthesised from academic and United Nations sources. In total, 64 research articles and book chapters were included for review, identifying 589 descriptions of degrowth food‐systems. The results were thematically synthesised to identify recurrent patterns, revealing the centrality of localised production and consumption practices to degrowth food‐systems, rooted in ecological and social care. Despite recurrent thematic patterns in the literature, future research can advance degrowth transition pathways by resolving tensions relating to the feasibility and modes of localised food provisioning, integrate more diverse cultural perspectives, establish stronger empirical foundations underpinning perspectives on ‘organic agriculture’, infrastructure, innovation and technology and examine the role of capitalist institutions in advancing degrowth transitions.

title: Natural sciences for post-growth in practice: low-tech iron oxide reduction under a concentrated light flux using urine-derived ammonia and hydrogen as reducers
abstract: A telling example of the green growth sociotechnical imaginary in natural sciences is the future of ‘green’ steel production, envisaged to grow based on a hypothetical massive deployment of low-carbon electricity. In this article, we show how a post-growth, low-tech framework can open up new innovation pathways towards sustainable futures of ironmaking. The low-tech processes that we envision aim at converting iron oxide into iron using readily available and renewable sources of reducing agents and energy: ammonia and hydrogen from urine, and concentrated sunlight. In our study, a solar concentrator simulator and synthetic urea were used as models to assess two ways of generating ammonia from urea for iron oxide reduction: i) the pyrolysis of solid urea inside the reduction reactor under concentrated light flux, and ii) the biocatalysed hydrolysis of urea by addition of urease-rich plant seeds – like soybeans or watermelon seeds – to an aqueous solution of urea mimicking urine. During the reduction of iron oxide, in situ mass spectrometry confirmed the decomposition of ammonia into hydrogen in presence of iron species. X-ray diffraction analysis of the resulting samples showed that the reduction yield successfully reached 90–98%. The global level of production of iron of such a process would be limited by urine production; estimates are provided and discussed. Parting from the green growth imaginary, our interdisciplinary work aims at reintegrating chemical processes into natural cycles, independent from both electricity and fossil fuels, and also at participating in opening up research to more diverse visions of the future.

title: How will we use our time in a future of sustainable wellbeing?
abstract: Time use analysis is an accessible and intuitive method for building an understanding of the greenhouse gas emissions footprint of lifestyles, and the ways in which these lifestyles impact our enjoyment and wellbeing. This study develops a novel methodology to estimate the emissions footprint and experienced wellbeing of daily life in 2050 in three global north countries (Finland, France, and the UK) from a time use perspective. Our modelling utilises time use analysis, experienced wellbeing data, direct emissions data, environmentally extended multiregional input-output analysis (MRIO), and scenario building. We first construct an ambitious 2050 scenario assuming a move to sufficiency-based household consumption of commodities and energy, dietary change, systemic changes to transport habits, technological change and cleaner production, and energy efficiency improvements. Despite modelling these ambitious changes out to 2050, we estimate that the emissions intensity of global north lifestyles will remain outside planetary boundaries. We then model experienced wellbeing and emissions in three time use scenarios, or ‘lifestyles’, for all three countries to understand how time use changes can improve wellbeing and lower lifestyle emissions. These scenarios are shaped by insights from functional time use theory (FTU), with further insights from the provisioning systems literature. We find that, though it is possible to improve our wellbeing and lower emissions through lifestyle change, further radical transformations are required to provisioning systems to bring emissions footprints within planetary boundaries. Moreover, without this transformation, some socially positive changes to time use may have unintended negative environmental effects.

title: When Firm Boundaries Meet Planetary Boundaries: Examining Corporate Land Use and Local Biodiversity With a Metacoupling Perspective
abstract: We investigate the collective interactions between corporate land use and biodiversity using the lenses of the metacoupling framework. Focusing on corporations in English and Welsh local councils between 2014 and 2019, we find that land use by intensive land use corporations is associated with reduced local species richness through intracoupling processes and causes negative outward spillover interactions with species richness in neighbouring areas via pericoupling processes. These intra- and pericoupling effects are stronger for ectotherms, small-bodied, and low‑dispersal species. We also find telecoupling effects where declines in ectotherms, terrestrial species, small-bodied species, and low-dispersal species richness intensify when local councils are part of the neighbouring, regional, and national road and rail network. International connections via seaports and airports are associated with reduced endotherm richness. By adding a spatial dimension to the analysis, this study outlines the importance of tracing the impacts of corporate activities beyond their conventional firm boundaries.

title: Assessing Strong Sustainability and Systemic Leadership in Corporate Climate Action: A Case Study From the Copper Mining Industry
journal: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes an exploratory instrument to assess how well organizations embed strong sustainability and systemic leadership into their climate mitigation efforts. After reviewing the case for strong sustainability in corporate climate action, it outlines a method, based on organizational psychologist Rae André's systemic climate leadership framework, to gauge how well companies (1) demonstrate basic climate literacy and risk awareness, (2) engage as agents of systemic change in their dealing with key external stakeholders, and (3) embrace a strong sustainability approach to decarbonization that prioritizes ecological science over economic expediency. The instrument is then tested via a case study of Freeport‐McMoRan, the world's largest publicly traded copper mining company. Freeport's approach to decarbonization was ascertained using document analysis of its website, corporate policies, sustainability reports, executive letters to stakeholders, interviews, and CDP questionnaires. Ultimately, although Freeport‐McMoRan's executive leadership has moderately demonstrated climate literacy, acknowledged climate risks, and selectively operated as an agent of systemic change through sectoral associations and with suppliers, it has not embraced strong sustainability to power its decarbonization efforts nor to advocate for climate policies. Applying the instrument produces a roadmap for researchers and executives looking to advance absolute decarbonization in large companies.

title: The role of sufficiency in aligning European sovereignty and sustainability in the lithium value chain
abstract: The transition towards low-carbon and digital technologies is set to profoundly reshape metals markets, particularly those required for battery manufacturing. Amid growing geoeconomic fragmentation, this shift is accelerating the implementation of public policies aimed at securing supply and strengthening the resilience of strategic technology value chains. In the European Union, the recently adopted Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) aims to ensure secure and sustainable access to critical raw materials. By integrating the entire lithium value chain into an Integrated Assessment Model, we analyse the interplay between lithium supply, demand, and recycling within decarbonisation scenarios. Our findings suggest significant challenges in meeting the CRMA reshoring targets without reducing industrial demand. We show that sufficiency strategies could help achieve these benchmarks, while cutting European lithium imports by at least 44% between 2030 and 2050 and reducing cumulative final demand by 1.2 Mt, a 46% decrease relative to current policy trajectories. Beyond securing supply, sufficiency reduces the energy footprint of the lithium chain, improves spatial extractive justice, and strengthens overall robustness under uncertainty. Integrating sufficiency into Europe’s material security framework offers a pathway to more closely align strategic autonomy with sustainability objectives.

title: Analyzing economic efficiency of global net primary production utilization within biosphere planetary boundary
keywords: human appropriation of net primary production

title: Navigating tensions in sufficiency-oriented businesses: coping strategies from a paradox theory perspective
abstract: Abstract Sufficiency calls for an absolute reduction of production and consumption volumes in affluent societies and is seen by many sustainability scholars as a fundamental strategy for businesses to tackle environmental and social crises. Existing literature emphasizes challenges that businesses experience when implementing sufficiency. However, the complex and paradoxical nature of implementing sufficiency has so far hindered scholars from giving a broad overview and description of challenges and conflicts that impede sufficiency-oriented businesses. This study applies a paradox approach to identify and systematize tensions in sufficiency-oriented businesses and solutions used to cope with them. Thirteen expert interviews with German-speaking sufficiency-oriented frontrunner businesses revealed eight paradoxes, which consist of tensions between the intentions of sufficiency-oriented frontrunners and opposing dominant structural aspects. For example, sufficiency practices are conflicting with consumerist culture, pressure for time and cost efficiency, or with neoliberal government objectives. The creativity and intrinsic motivation of the employees and management, however, help these sufficiency-oriented frontrunners to find solutions to the paradoxes and continue to prioritize sufficiency in spite of paradoxical situations. Collaboration with other stakeholders appears as an essential resolution strategy to cope with the tensions. With the help of paradox theory, this study systematizes for the first time the variety of paradoxical tensions and situations that sufficiency-oriented businesses face and helps future practitioners and researchers navigate these tensions. It gives an overview of the complex reality of implementing practices that oppose the status quo and illustrates the necessity of coping mechanisms and perseverance strategies for creating long-lasting and sustainable impact.

title: Integrating Theory and Practice in Regenerative Supply Chain Management: An Integrative Review and Use‐Case Synthesis
abstract: ABSTRACT This integrative review explores the evolution of sustainability in supply chain management and positions regenerative supply chain within the strong sustainability paradigm. It adopts a transdisciplinary approach, unfolding in two parallel stages. The first stage includes an integrative literature review that draws on disciplines beyond supply chain management, including organisational studies, industrial ecology, agriculture, tourism and the built environment. The second stage synthesises use cases of strategies successfully implemented by firms worldwide. The review also offers a working definition of regenerative supply chain, and advances the discourse on sustainability in supply chain management. By synthesising existing scholarship on regenerative supply chains alongside the broader paradigmatic shift towards regeneration, and by examining the strategies firms use, this review introduces the phased‐gate approach, which forms five sequential phases that bridge theory and practice. This review specifically focuses on contributing to SDG ‐12, 13, 14 and 15.

title: Energy, surplus and the economic process
abstract: This paper analyses the economic process through the concept of surplus, combining insights from ecological economics, Marxist political economy and anthropology. Humans, we argue, appropriate surplus energy with their labor from nature and apply it to transform matter into goods and services, with entropy increasing along the way. How societies distribute and expend their surpluses gives them some of their signature features. In hierarchical societies, the ruling classes control a great share of the surplus and expend it in ways that reproduce their power. Economic growth, a distinctive feature of capitalist civilization, is the result of the ruling capitalist class investing surplus in the means of production in order to make more surplus. Surplus is extracted both via technological innovation that increases productivity and by social domination that reduces the share of surplus that goes back to workers or nature. Growth, however, is not only a material process but also a hegemonic story told by the capitalist class to dress its private interest as general interest, legitimating control over the destiny of surplus. Our framework proposes a political, ecological-economic theory of growth, provides a foundation for analyzing degrowth, and sheds new light on longstanding debates between ecological economists and Marxists.

title: Life-Affirming Organizations (LAOs): An Integrated Framework of Normative Foundations, Structural Reconfigurations, and Contextualized Enactment
abstract: Critical sustainability and organization studies challenge the dominant neoliberal paradigm by advancing alternative forms of organizing that contest anthropocentric assumptions and uphold socio-ecological integrity, thereby supporting life-affirmation. This conceptual paper develops an integrated Life-Affirming Organizations framework that articulates how the normative foundations of life-affirmation can be translated into contextualized structural reconfigurations of organizing. Drawing on life-affirming principles as an overarching interpretive lens and mobilizing an institutional lens to account for organizational transformation, the article adopts a reflexive, multi-perspective approach to review, analyze, and integrate insights from Humanistic Management and Regenerative Development. These two heterodox traditions, rooted in ethical business scholarship and living systems thinking, address complementary yet tension-laden dimensions of life-affirming organizing. Conceptually, the Life-Affirming Organizations framework advances critical organization studies by articulating life-affirming organizing as a coherent structural configuration rather than a set of normative aspirations. Practically, the institutional lens enables understanding the structural barriers, intrinsic challenges, and adaptive strategies involved in transitioning toward life-affirming, context-embedded organizational forms, highlighting how organizations must navigate trade-offs between competing logics.

title: Startups’ sustainable business models as reference points for achieving the optimal integration of value networks
abstract: For startups, the success of sustainable business models (SBMs) hinges on building integrated value networks, yet conventional network characteristics like breadth and depth often fall short of capturing the degree of integration, and how to achieve such integration remains unclear. This paper explores how stakeholder engagement strategies enable startups to achieve optimal stakeholder integration for SBMs. An exploratory, qualitative study identifies two characteristics – stakeholder resistance and resource flow – to capture the degree of network integration, highlighting that the level of incorporating a sustainability mission into SBMs determines the optimal degrees of both characteristics. Then, this study reveals four engagement strategies – empathy, confidence, exploration and implementation – that influence these characteristics to achieve an optimal integration. Specifically, startups with a strong sustainability mission require low-resistance & high resource integration; those with a medium sustainability mission need moderate levels of both; and weak sustainability mission startups require high-resistance & low resource integration.

title: Wealth taxes for an eco-social transition: How different tax designs align with post-growth goals
abstract: Wealth taxes are frequently proposed within the post-growth policy literature, but evaluations of their alignment with post-growth goals, and empirical estimates of their potential effects, are lacking. We contribute to this literature by examining the extent to which different wealth tax designs can contribute to four goals of a post-growth transition: redistributing wealth; eradicating extreme wealth; curbing rent-seeking; and reducing CO 2 emissions. The analysis is based on microsimulation modelling, using household-level data from 18 countries of the 2017 EU Household Finance and Consumption Survey. It shows that broad-based net wealth taxes with lower thresholds and higher rates are most effective for maximising revenue, reducing top 10% wealth shares, limiting extreme wealth, and lowering inequality-related CO₂ emissions; more targeted net wealth taxes with higher thresholds and rates maximise progressivity and reduce top 1% wealth concentration; while taxes on financial and investment property wealth tend to be most effective at curbing rent extraction (all else equal). However, we also identify trade-offs and conflicts between different tax designs and goals. As a result, a broader package of policies will be necessary to navigate these conflicts and mitigate the limitations inherent in any single wealth tax design.

title: Modeling for post-growth: Backcasting radical futures
abstract: Economic models are more than technical instruments: they are lenses that shape our understanding of reality and our ability to address contemporary challenges. They embed ethical commitments, political assumptions, and institutional framings that influence their outputs. We illustrate how normative and positive modeling approaches anchor their projections in existing economic structures through what we call structural induction. This effect is further reinforced by the way models frame scenarios. In the context of post-growth, these framing effects limit the capacity to explore radical narratives. To overcome these limitations, we advocate a backcasting approach, beginning with detailed qualitative narratives of proposed futures and using models iteratively to check their consistency and explore them quantitatively. In this way, models are used as exploratory tools, probing uncertain terrain rather than producing projections. This approach calls for the development of comprehensive and shared post-growth narratives. We then propose a conceptual classification of models, based on Daly's ends-means spectrum, to cover the range of post-growth concerns: need-oriented modeling, social and physical provisioning systems modeling, and biophysical modeling. Reviewing recent modeling exercises through this lens, we observe that biophysical modeling is gaining increasing attention, while need-oriented modeling remains underexplored despite its central importance for representing post-growth futures. Finally, we discuss the need for the modeling community to adopt a critical stance toward models and to explicitly define criteria for their validity.

title: From utopian impulse to urban engagement: The role of doughnut economics in shaping residents' participation in smart cities
abstract: Smart cities are often framed through techno-utopian narratives, yet their capacity to support sustainable transitions depends on residents' engagement. This article examines how the transformative utopian impulse and support for the principles of Doughnut Economics shape residents' intention to participate in smart city projects. Drawing on a survey of 645 residents in five French cities (Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Lille and Toulouse), we estimate a model using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) combined with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) to distinguish sufficient from necessary causal relations. PLS-SEM results show that the transformative utopian impulse significantly influences participatory intention, both directly and indirectly through support for Doughnut Economics principles. NCA complements these findings by revealing that both constructs operate as necessary conditions for high levels of participatory intention, with support for Doughnut Economics emerging as the most critical precondition for high levels of participatory intention: while it contributes relatively little as a direct average driver of participation, its absence effectively prevents residents from reaching the highest levels of engagement. This “axiological” threshold effect indicates that commitment to post-growth principles shifts from secondary to indispensable as participation intensifies. The study advances urban governance research by moving beyond the opposition between technology-centric smart city agendas and post-growth urbanism: Doughnut Economics functions as an intermediary normative framework translating utopian aspirations into more concrete forms of urban engagement. For practitioners, the results highlight that participatory mechanisms must be coupled with coherent value frameworks if smart city programmes are to mobilise residents for transformative and sustainability-oriented projects.

title: The Adoption of Sufficiency Practices in Sustainability‐Oriented Businesses: A Mixed‐Methods Study of Enablers, Challenges, and Benefits
abstract: ABSTRACT Sufficiency is increasingly seen as a necessary complement to efficiency and circularity strategies to help prevent the transgression of planetary boundaries. However, empirical evidence on their broader relevance in business remains limited. This study uses an exploratory mixed‐methods design to assess the adoption of sufficiency practices, as well as their enablers, challenges, and benefits in sustainability‐oriented companies in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Findings show that internal sufficiency practices focus on aligning organizational culture and leadership with sufficiency principles, alongside adjustments to production processes. Externally, companies emphasize customer engagement and contributions to systemic change. Adoption is driven by the commitment, knowledge, and values of organizational members, while challenges include resource constraints, profitability tensions, and limited political support. In addition, the study highlights strong normative and competitive benefits of sufficiency practices and provides practical insights for businesses and policymakers aiming to foster supportive conditions for advancing sufficiency in business.

title: Assessing the balance and correlation of global sustainable development within a safe and just operating space
Between refuse and recycle: asymmetric polarization in circular economy representations
abstract: The concept of the circular economy ( CE ) has gained increasing prominence over the past decade, yet its meaning remains ambiguous and often diverges from the original vision of early CE pioneers. Understanding how this ambiguity shapes public perceptions is critical for the effective design and implementation of CE policies. Drawing on a survey of 1281 respondents in France, this study examines individuals' familiarity with CE , their spontaneous definitions, and their prioritization of circular strategies using the 5R hierarchy (refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle). The results reveal a strong and asymmetric polarization of CE representations, structured around the acceptance or rejection of the refuse (sufficiency) lever. Recycling and reuse dominate spontaneous definitions, while reuse and recycling are prioritized when respondents explicitly rank CE levers. By contrast, refuse remains marginal despite its central role in strong circularity approaches. Socio-economic characteristics do not robustly explain this polarization. However, respondents whose preferences align more closely with strong circularity—consistent with the pioneers’ vision—report higher levels of pro-environmental behaviors and stronger support for CE-related public policies. These findings highlight a persistent gap between weak and strong circularity representations and suggest important implications for CE communication strategies and public policymaking.

title: Understandings of sufficiency: A phenomenography on the sufficiency movement in Finland
abstract: Sufficiency is increasingly recognised as necessary to address the environmental crises, yet the concept still lacks clarity. Given the importance of a strong public opinion prioritising environmental concerns, I study understandings of sufficiency in an environmental movement context. I build on recent studies calling for further empirical research, noting that an environmental movement perspective is rare in sufficiency studies. This article aims to clarify understandings of sufficiency in the Finnish sufficiency movement ‘Kohtuusliike’. For that purpose, I conducted semi-structured interviews with 16 persons active in the movement and analysed the interviews utilising a phenomenographic approach. The main findings include four understandings of sufficiency: as (a) a necessity (material and mental), (b) an analytical tool (criticism and advocacy), (c) reframing change and (d) compromising action. My main contribution is having conducted the first study on sufficiency understandings in an environmental movement context, presenting a broad and systematic approach to sufficiency, including bringing up a sufficiency dimension that seems to have gained little attention in previous studies: nature relation. I conclude by suggesting that the derived understandings support clarifying the sufficiency concept, including operationalising sufficiency more broadly in an environmental movement context concerned with environmental and social boundaries. In a broader social–ecological transformation perspective, the study focuses on persons that can be characterised as sufficiency role models in an affluent country context.

title: Life-cycle assessment and triple planetary crisis: A review on methodological gaps and potential future improvements
Technological ambivalence and degrowth
abstract: This article analyses technological ambivalence and its implications for degrowth scholarship and practice. We critically examine and reject the assumption of ontological ambivalence, in which technologies are understood as indeterminate with respect to their socio-ecological conditions and consequences. We distinguish this from epistemological ambivalence, in which ambivalence refers to indecisiveness in human interpretations, experiences and valuations of technology. We show that parts of contemporary degrowth scholarship implicitly rely on an ontological reading of technological ambivalence in discussions of technological solutions, such as lower-carbon energy systems. Drawing on critical realism and philosophical materialism, we argue that technologies are materially and biophysically real and have determinate conditions of existence, including unavoidable environmental impacts and socially uneven conditions of production. On this basis, we contend that ambivalence should be understood as a feature of human interpretation and valuation rather than an intrinsic property of technological objects. We suggest that degrowth scholarship reject ontological accounts of technological ambivalence in favour of epistemological ones and adopt a more critical stance toward the assumption that advanced modern technologies can be made environmentally sustainable.

title: Food System Through the Lens of a Circular Society: A Transdisciplinary Approach to Integrating Literature and Practice
abstract: ABSTRACT Circular society (CS) conceptualises circularity as a multi‐level governance transformation involving the redistribution of authority, responsibility and coordination across socio‐institutional systems. Yet the concept remains insufficiently operationalised in empirical research. This study advances the empirical operationalisation of CS as a governance‐diagnostic framework within food systems. Through a transdisciplinary design, it combines a scoping review of 238 studies and stakeholder workshops involving 68 participants to map actor‐role distributions and identify transition leverage domains. The literature mapping shows that circular actions are concentrated at meso and micro levels, with limited engagement at macro and exo governance levels. In contrast, stakeholders located transformative leverage at macro and exo levels, prioritising procurement mandates, fiscal instruments and regulatory redesign while identifying cross‐level coordination deficits as key constraints. The divergence between literature emphasis and stakeholder prioritisation exposes institutional asymmetries in circular transition pathways. By integrating literature‐based actor mapping with stakeholder‐based prioritisation, the study operationalises circular society as a governance‐diagnostic framework for identifying leverage domains in circular food system transitions.

title: Democratically planned degrowth: Modeling for rapid climate crisis mitigation
Post-growth and the North-South divide: A stock-flow consistent scenario analysis
Sufficiency in principle and practice: An operational definition and typology
abstract: Sufficiency is emerging as a necessary concept as safe and just Earth system boundaries are increasingly transgressed, yet its definition and operationalisation remain fragmented. In this paper, we provide an operational definition for the concept, defining sufficiency as a state of enoughness that avoids both deficiency and excess in relation to fair social and ecological limits. Then, we develop a typology for the classification and analysis of practical sufficiency measures through a theory-informed content analysis of 1,101 proposed measures drawn from three diverse datasets. The resulting typology identifies five distinct types of sufficiency measures: quantitative, qualitative, use, sharing, and steering. To demonstrate the applicability of our typology, we test it against 33 policies presented in the “Sufficiency Manifesto” for the European Union, classifying policies based on the sufficiency measure type and whether they targeted the household, private, or public sector. Our analysis shows that all five types of sufficiency measures were present, though unevenly, with sharing measures least represented. This demonstrates how the typology can reveal patterns or gaps in current approaches and highlight opportunities for more comprehensive strategies. By developing an operational definition of sufficiency, clarifying its implications in both principle and practice, and offering a typological tool for analysing sufficiency measures across sectors and scales, this study advances the conceptual foundations and operationalisation of sufficiency, providing an empirically grounded framework for its systematic application.

title: Limits to growth revisited: System dynamics simulations of global economic developments and distributional implications in the 21st century
abstract: We use a system dynamics environment-economy model to explore how multiple limits to growth may affect global economic output and consumption across different social classes until 2100. Based on a five-dimensional scenario space, we simulate global economic development in 120 scenarios that differ in labor productivity growth, per-capita consumption growth, fossil resource availability, climate change severity, and climate system sensitivity. In 92% of the simulations, output peaks and then declines persistently. Excluding scenarios without climate impacts, output in 2100 is 15–70% lower than in 2019. Scenarios with low labor productivity and consumption growth experience earlier peaks at lower levels and moderate output declines. In contrast, scenarios with high labor productivity and consumption growth show faster and longer periods of growth but eventually face economic collapse. While resource depletion and climate damages act as stressors, most simulations indicate that growth ultimately halts and reverses due to a shortage of labor hours. During the phase of unintentional economic degrowth, economic convergence and redistribution reduce consumption in high-income countries to values 3–4 times lower than initial consumption levels, while middle- and low-income countries return to consumption levels similar to those at the start of the simulations. Poverty reduction in poorer regions ends as global output peaks, while environmental destabilization caused by economic growth threatens development opportunities beyond the 21st century.

title: Modelling degrowth policies with system dynamics: Towards policy coherence
abstract: • We simulate degrowth policy interactions in a high-income country. • Degrowth policies can reduce environmental pressures and advance social equity. • Isolated policies create trade-offs; coherent policy packages can resolve them. • Producing less while redistributing more improves social-ecological outcomes. • Short-term fiscal feasibility contrasts with long-term public debt challenges.

title: Quantifying overconsumption: Deriving safe and equitable benchmarks to evaluate the environmental footprints of Germany's bioeconomy
abstract: The transition to a sustainable bioeconomy joins socio-economic and environmental goals. Getting there requires monitoring national consumption levels in relation to sustainability metrics.
